newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland works on plan to join EMU in 2006-2008.
newsitem.headline: Poland works on plan to join EMU in 2006-2008.

text.p: Finance Minister Grzegorz Kolodko said on Friday he was preparing a new long-term economic plan aimed at preparing Poland to join the European Union in five years and adopt the euro as its currency between 2006 and 2008.

Kolodko said the scheme, named "Euro 2006," will provide for adjusting the economy to meet five Maastricht criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU), regarding the budget deficit, inflation, public debt, interest and exchange rates.
"It seems we have a chance to enter the EU as a full memeber between 2000 and 2002... and that we could have a chance to join the monetary union between 2006 and 2008," he told a news conference.

Poland, now an EU associate member, hopes to begin accession negotiations with Brussels in early 1998 and Western leaders have said it could join the community in 2000-2002 as one of the first countries from the former Soviet bloc.

The European Commission praises Poland's macroeconomic achievements, such as its low budget deficit and sustained growth, but criticises delays in restructuring heavy industries and plans to protect them longer than earlier agreed.
Poland must also reform its costly subsidised social security system, inherited from the communist era, if it wants to cope with inflation, which remains high.
Kolodko said his programme would envisage slashing annual inflation to five percent in 2000 and three percent in 2002 from October's 19.5 percent.
He said the three percent inflation target was crucial to allow Poland to meet other criteria for taking part in a single European currency.
Poland now meets two Maastricht criteria, having a budget deficit to GDP ratio below three percent and a public debt to GDP ratio below 60 percent.
Kolodko said it was too early to give more details of his plan but that the 1997 budget draft was in line with the strategy of integration with the EU.

The bill aims to cut annual inflation to 13 percent in December 1997 while preserving economic growth at 5.5 percent and reducing unemployment to 12.9 percent from 13.6 percent at end-1996. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
